trie-intro.introduction: A Trie (Prefix Tree) is a tree-like data structure used to store a dynamic set of strings. It is highly optimized for fast retrieval, autocomplete features, and spell checking.
trie-intro.intuition: Think of looking up a word in a dictionary. You first find the page for the first letter, then the section for the second letter, and so on. A Trie structures data exactly like this.

walkthrough.description: Each node contains an array of 26 pointers (one for each letter) and a boolean `isEndOfWord` flag.
Iterate through characters. If the child node doesn't exist, create it. Move to the child. At the end, set `isEndOfWord = true`.
Iterate through characters. If a child doesn't exist, return false. At the end, return the `isEndOfWord` flag.

dryRun.output: Search 'cat' -> true. Search 'ca' -> false (but prefix is true).
steps: Search 'ca': root -> c -> a. End of 'ca' is not true. Return false.

complexities.analysis: Time is O(L) where L is the length of the word. Space can be large if there are many unique words with few common prefixes.

mistakes: Using a Hash Map for dictionary problems when prefix matching is required. Hash Maps cannot do prefix matching efficiently.
edgeCases: Searching a string longer than any inserted string
tips: Always clarify the character set. If it's just lowercase english letters, an array of size 26 is best. If it's ASCII, size 256. If unicode, use a Hash Map in the node.

design-add-search.introduction: Design a data structure that supports adding new words and finding if a string matches any previously added string. The search query may contain the dot '.' character which acts as a wildcard matching any single letter.
design-add-search.intuition: Standard Trie search, but when we encounter a '.', we must recursively search ALL 26 possible children of the current node.

walkthrough.description: Recursive DFS search starting from the root node and index 0 of the word.
If char is '.', loop over all 26 children. If any recursive search returns true, return true.

steps: Search '.ad': At root, '.' means check children 'b', 'd', 'm'.
Check child 'b'. Next char 'a' matches. Next 'd' matches. True.

complexities.analysis: Time complexity for a word of all wildcards '.....' is O(26^L). Space is O(L) for recursion stack plus the Trie storage.

mistakes: Using BFS instead of DFS for the wildcard search. BFS can use too much memory storing states for long strings of wildcards.
edgeCases: Search string consists entirely of dots
tips: This is the exact same logic used in Word Search II for moving in a grid.

word-search-ii.introduction: Given an m x n board of characters and a list of strings words, return all words on the board.
word-search-ii.intuition: Running standard DFS for every word from every cell is O(W * M * N * 4^L), which is too slow. Instead, we insert all words into a Trie, and run DFS from every cell simultaneously checking against the Trie.

walkthrough.description: Insert all words into a Trie. Store the actual word string at the `isEnd` node for easy extraction.
Iterate through every cell (r, c). Start DFS passing the root of the Trie.
If the current character doesn't exist in the current Trie node, stop (Prune). If it's a valid word node, add to results and mark `isEnd = false` to prevent duplicates.

steps: DFS from (0,0) 'o'. Matches root->'o'. Move to 'a'. Matches 'o'->'a'. Move to 't'. Matches 'a'->'t'. Move to 'h'. Matches 't'->'h'. Word found!

complexities.analysis: Time complexity drops because we only explore paths in the grid that actually form prefixes of words in our dictionary. We use 3 directions not 4, because we don't go back.
